image_targets.codex: recovered Class-III collar ring on a bench, config plate open, sample lot number stamped in the metal, no faces and no photographs in frame
image_targets.scanner_thumbnail: single audio channel on a repair bench display showing two overlapping voice traces on one track

en_US.title: Comfort Channel Test, 620 Metres
en_US.scanner: Recorder intact. 41 seconds recoverable. Confidence 84 percent. Two voices on one channel. Limit: cannot separate synthesised track from live track.
en_US.in_game_wiki:
The comfort channel is a factory option on the Class-III and Class-IV, not a fault, and it shipped by the crate.

A suit configured for it carries a sample lot in the guidance field instead of the stock voice. The lot number is stamped on the collar config plate and points into a personnel file, usually a family channel recording the holder submitted himself.

Below about five hundred metres on Mix 4 the channel stops being furniture. Judgement narrows, the recording keeps its cadence, and a slowed holder will answer a voice he can still correctly name as a recording.

Fourteen of the sixteen recovered suits with the option enabled worked the same depth band.

Assessment: read the collar plate before diving a salvaged suit. That channel has priority over the hazard tone.
en_US.terminal: AUDIO ITEM 44-AL-0118. FEATURE: COMFORT VOICE CHANNEL, FACTORY OPTION. SAMPLE LOT: HOLDER SUPPLIED. CLASS: MORALE HARDWARE, NON-CRITICAL. FAILURE REVIEW: OUT OF SCOPE. HOLDER STATUS: ASSET REASSIGNMENT.
en_US.field_note: Morale hardware, non-critical, and it was the last thing still talking to him at six hundred metres. Read the collar plate before you dive a salvaged suit, because that channel has priority over the hazard tone.
en_US.audio:
-- no, say the second part again. The part about the gate.

[COMFORT CHANNEL] Come in by the tide bell, Tomas. Come in by the tide bell.

That is not her. I know exactly what that is, I loaded the lot myself in forty-one off the family channel. Six hundred and twenty metres, Mix 4, and it still lands.

For the record: I am past marker nine, my hands are slow, the board is green, and I am going to finish the run. The option functions as written. Put that in the file.

Say it again.
en_US.external_site_article:
Class-III and Class-IV pressure suits shipped with an optional guidance voice drawn from a holder-supplied sample rather than the stock synthesiser. Aegir salvage crews report the option enabled on recovered Sector 44 units, identifiable from a sample lot number stamped on the collar config plate.

Recovered audio from HECTON-8 includes holders using the channel at depths where inert gas effects are documented, and doing so with the recording correctly identified as a recording. Deep Reach classified the option as non-critical morale hardware, a category excluded from failure review, which is why the record contains no assessment of how it behaves at depth.
en_US.external_site: Class-III and Class-IV pressure suits shipped with an optional guidance voice drawn from a holder-supplied sample rather than the stock synthesiser. Aegir salvage crews report the option enabled on recovered Sector 44 units, identifiable from a sample lot number stamped on the collar config plate.

image_targets.codex: colony credential reader beside a sealed pressure door, palm plate worn smooth, single amber attempt counter lit, water line partway up the frame
image_targets.scanner_thumbnail: reader display holding a correct holder code above a request line for a school certificate

en_US.title: Reissue Request, Door 9
en_US.scanner: Governor exchange recovered, two channels. Confidence 62 percent. Hazard: presentation loop still active on this reader. Limit: holder record reads valid.
en_US.in_game_wiki:
Atlas-6 answers credential requests out of the wrong field of the correct file.

The holder code comes back right. That is the tell, and it is why crews kept trying. A local reader that has lost you returns a null holder; the governor confirms you by code and then asks for a document from further down the same personnel block, a school certificate, a dependant's dental chart, a guardian countersignature. Minor records and authorisations were stored in one block and the field pointer slipped.

It never asks twice for the same document. Every document it asks for was issued before the holder turned twelve.

Attempts are counted aloud, one of three, and the third closes the reader for the rest of the shift.

Assessment: request by bay number and audit line. The word present starts the count.
en_US.terminal: SCHEMA TICKET AT6-2214-09. SYMPTOM: MINOR AND DEPENDANT RECORDS PRESENTED AS CREDENTIALS. FIELD POINTER: PERSONNEL BLOCK. CLASS: SCHEMA FAULT, LOW SEVERITY. REMEDY: DEFERRED. BAY 4 UPPER: SEALED, PRESSURE VARIANCE.
en_US.field_note: Low severity means nobody had to fix it. Give a governor a bay number and an audit line; the moment you say present, you have lost that reader for the shift.
en_US.audio:
-- reissue on door 9, Bay 4 upper, holder I-2214, pressure authorisation, standard.

[ATLAS-6] HOLDER I-2214 CONFIRMED. PRESENT CREDENTIAL: SWIMMING CERTIFICATE, GRADE TWO, ISSUED 2118, GUARDIAN COUNTERSIGNED. HOLD DOCUMENT TO THE READER. ATTEMPT ONE OF THREE.

It has the right file. Same file, further down.

[ATLAS-6] ATTEMPT TWO OF THREE. PRESENT CREDENTIAL: DEPENDANT DENTAL SURVEY, MOLAR CHART, ISSUED 2119, GUARDIAN COUNTERSIGNED.

Twenty-five metres, no hands on the wall, I was nine years old. And my palm is flat on the reader, because that is what you do when it says present.

Put a schema fault on the board tonight. Bay 4 upper has water behind it and the door is --

[ATLAS-6] ATTEMPT THREE OF THREE. PRESENT CREDENTIAL: GUARDIAN SIGNATURE CARD, ISSUED 2116. HOLD DOCUMENT TO THE READER. THANK YOU.
en_US.external_site_article:
Atlas-6, the damaged factory-governor in Sector 44, still answers credential requests on colony readers. Recovered exchanges show the governor confirming a holder code correctly and then requesting a document from elsewhere in the same personnel block, including records created while the holder was a minor.

Deep Reach filed the behaviour as a low-severity schema fault with remedy deferred. Aegir salvage practice on HECTON-8 is to phrase a request as a bay number and an audit line, since a presentation sequence is counted to three attempts and then locks the reader for the remainder of the shift.
en_US.external_site: Atlas-6, the damaged factory-governor in Sector 44, still answers credential requests on colony readers. Recovered exchanges show the governor confirming a holder code correctly and then requesting a document from elsewhere in the same personnel block, including records created while the holder was a minor.

image_targets.codex: single bolt head under a washer throwing a narrow white atomised cone a metre into a flooded machine gallery, graduated sump collar on the far wall
image_targets.scanner_thumbnail: sump collar graduation in millimetres with a wet line across it and a chalk mark below the line

en_US.title: Bolt 14, West Rib
en_US.scanner: Voice log, 64 seconds. Confidence 91 percent. Bolt seat behind this wall reads seated. Limit: weep below sensor threshold.
en_US.in_game_wiki:
A weeping bolt at nine megapascals does not drip. It stands a white atomised cone off the washer, roughly a metre of cone for every eight megapascals behind it.

The compartment hands you a clock for nothing. Sump collars are graduated in millimetres, and two readings an hour turn the weep into a fill rate and the fill rate into standing time. Bay 9 ran one hundred and ten millimetres an hour against a two point four metre ceiling, and the rate climbed as the thread opened.

Bolt 14 on the west rib failed first in three bays carrying different loads. In the third bay the bolt was new that year.

Assessment: read the collar twice an hour and price the compartment against your own window rather than against the requisition class.
en_US.terminal: WORK ORDER 44-RIB-0140. ITEM: BOLT 14, WEST RIB, BAY 9. FINDING: PRESSURE VARIANCE, CLASS 2. LEAD TIME: 6 DAYS. INTERIM: MONITOR SUMP COLLAR. COMPARTMENT: RETAINED IN SERVICE.
en_US.field_note: Nineteen hours against a six-day lead time, and the compartment stayed in service. Price a room in your own window and read the collar twice an hour.
en_US.audio:
-- it is not a drip. Stop writing drip. Bolt head 14, west rib, hairline under the washer, standing a white cone a metre into the room. Eight point eight megapascals on the other side of that washer.

Sump collar read four hundred and ten millimetres on the hour. Five hundred and twenty now. One ten an hour and climbing as the thread opens. Ceiling is two point four.

So nineteen hours of compartment, eleven of standing. Rib bolt is a Class 2. Six days.

Madsen, write the number, not the word. Nineteen against six, in the box, in ink. Then photograph the collar with the chalk mark in frame, because the day crew will say I moved the chalk.
en_US.external_site_article:
Bolt-seat weeps in the Drowned Factories present as a standing white cone rather than as dripping water, because a hairline path at eight to nine megapascals atomises the flow. Cone length is used in the field as a rough indicator of the differential behind it.

Recovered work orders from Sector 44 show compartments retained in service while a Class 2 requisition ran a six-day lead time against fill rates that removed standing room inside a single shift. Deep Reach recorded the condition as pressure variance and instructed monitoring of the sump collar.
en_US.external_site: Bolt-seat weeps in the Drowned Factories present as a standing white cone rather than as dripping water, because a hairline path at eight to nine megapascals atomises the flow. Cone length is used in the field as a rough indicator of the differential behind it.

image_targets.codex: printed telemetry strip clipped to a bench with a handwritten number in ink beside the printed column, bare wrist and open glove seam in frame
image_targets.scanner_thumbnail: suit alarm board showing every band green with a bay clock reflected in the glass

en_US.title: Wrist Count Against The Board
en_US.scanner: Log intact with attached telemetry strip. Confidence 88 percent. All alarm bands nominal. Limit: handwritten annexe not machine-readable.
en_US.in_game_wiki:
A green board is a claim about the alarm band, not a measurement of the holder.

Calibration drift widens that band until the warning falls outside it, so the display holds green through the whole excursion and the printed strip agrees with itself afterwards. The body has no such setting. A pulse taken at the glove seam against a bay clock, counted twice, is analog data no firmware revision can widen, which is why a strip carrying an ink column beside the printed one is the only telemetry in Sector 44 worth carrying out.

Recorded drift only ever moves toward green.

Assessment: write the wrist count in ink beside the printout, both numbers, ink first. A board that has never left green has not measured anything.
en_US.terminal: TELEMETRY EXCEPTION 44-TE-0771. UNIT: ALARM BOARD, SERIAL 3308. FINDING: ALARM BAND WITHIN CALIBRATION DRIFT. HOLDER ANNOTATION: MANUAL, INK, NOT ADMITTED. CLASS: DATA INTEGRITY SATISFIED. ACTION: NONE.
en_US.field_note: Calibration drift is their word for an alarm somebody turned off. Put both numbers in your log, board and wrist, ink first, because the next diver reads your log and not their form.
en_US.audio:
-- board is green. Board has been green for forty minutes.

I am counting one hundred and thirty at the wrist, through the glove seam, against the bay clock, twice, and I get the same number twice. Cartridge is stamped eleven hours and it has run nine.

So either my hand is lying or the band got widened. One of those is on a form somewhere with a signature under it.

I am putting the wrist number in ink beside the printout. Morita, if the green one goes up alone, that was a choice somebody made.

Whoever pulls this cartridge: the ink column is mine and the printed column is theirs. Keep both, and do not let anybody file the strip without the ink.
en_US.external_site_article:
Suit alarm boards report whether a reading falls inside a calibration band rather than reporting the reading. Where the band has been widened, the display remains nominal across an excursion, a condition Deep Reach records describe as calibration drift.

HECTON-8 salvage practice is to record a manually counted pulse at the glove seam alongside the printed telemetry and to keep both figures in the log. Deep Reach exception files from Sector 44 note holder annotations in ink as not admitted, with the telemetry record closed and no action taken.
en_US.external_site: Suit alarm boards report whether a reading falls inside a calibration band rather than reporting the reading. Where the band has been widened, the display remains nominal across an excursion, a condition Deep Reach records describe as calibration drift.

image_targets.codex: vent plume leaning almost flat downstream at working depth, clear water directly above the throat, silt streamers showing the bottom current direction
image_targets.scanner_thumbnail: suit thermal overlay showing a cool column above a vent and a hot band offset to one side

en_US.title: Throat 12, Forty Metres Downstream
en_US.scanner: Recorder heat-damaged. 38 seconds recoverable. Confidence 55 percent. Hazard: local water 61 C. Limit: thermal overlay updates every 9 seconds.
en_US.in_game_wiki:
Vent heat in the Thermal Fields travels sideways before it travels up.

A cold bottom set runs across the throats between four and five thousand metres and shears the plume over, so the hot water is not above the hole, it is downstream of the hole, held at working depth in a band forty to sixty metres across. Nothing above the throat reads warm. The suit overlay resolves the band about nine seconds late, and at swim speed nine seconds is most of the crossing.

The band keeps its shape for hours after the throat goes quiet.

Assessment: cross a vent field upstream into the cold set even when it costs the shortcut. Outer plate above sixty means look at the gloves before looking at the display.
en_US.terminal: FIELD NOTE 44-TF-0496. LOCATION: 4900 M, THROAT 12, DOWNSTREAM 40 M. FINDING: PLUME DISPLACEMENT, LATERAL. OUTER PLATE: 61 C. INJURY CLASSIFICATION: EQUIPMENT DEGRADATION. ROUTE ADVISORY: PENDING.
en_US.field_note: Route advisory pending for forty-three years. Cross upstream into the cold, and if your plate passes sixty, look at your gloves right then and not at the display.
en_US.audio:
-- back off. Back off, it is not over the vent. Four thousand nine hundred, forty metres east and downhill of throat 12, and the outer plate just went to sixty-one.

The cold set is shearing the whole plume sideways. The heat is not above the hole, it is downstream of the hole, and it is sitting at my depth.

Overlay is nine seconds behind me. Nine seconds is the crossing.

Cross a vent field upstream. Upstream, into the cold, every time, even if it costs you the run.

My left glove has gone stiff. I am not going to look at it yet.

[RECORDER] CASE TEMPERATURE ABOVE LIMIT. WRITE PROTECT ENGAGED. CHANNEL CLOSED AT 38 SECONDS.
en_US.external_site_article:
Vent fields between four and five thousand metres on HECTON-8 are crossed by a cold bottom current that displaces plumes laterally. Hot water is therefore found downstream of a throat at working depth rather than directly above it, in bands reported at forty to sixty metres across.

Suit thermal overlays resolve these bands with a lag of several seconds, which is significant at swim speed, and field practice is to cross upstream into the cold set. A Deep Reach field note from Sector 44 records an outer plate reading of 61 C and classifies the associated injury as equipment degradation.
en_US.external_site: Vent fields between four and five thousand metres on HECTON-8 are crossed by a cold bottom current that displaces plumes laterally. Hot water is therefore found downstream of a throat at working depth rather than directly above it, in bands reported at forty to sixty metres across.

image_targets.codex: sonar repeater in a cramped instrument bay, bearing needle steady on a lit arc, range readout blank, no target rendered anywhere in frame
image_targets.scanner_thumbnail: printed sonar strip with six aligned bearing marks and an empty range column

en_US.title: Six Returns, No Range
en_US.scanner: Log with sonar strip attached. Confidence 77 percent. Six returns, bearing only. Limit: range field empty, logged as parameter exception.
en_US.in_game_wiki:
A bearing with an empty range field is a reading, not a broken set.

Mark 9 active sets carry an upper limit on target extent. A return above that limit fails the range solution, so the gate discards the range field while the bearing channel, indifferent to extent, keeps working. Six returns inside an arc second of each other is not noise. It is six good measurements of direction and a refusal to state distance.

Bearing drift under your own motion is the only ranging left. Four degrees in eleven minutes while swimming means station-keeping.

Two sets on different hulls, run the same hour, both refused range and disagreed on bearing by eleven degrees.

Assessment: kill the active set, change depth rather than heading, and log the full bearing series. The gate limit has not been raised since 2147.
en_US.terminal: SENSOR TICKET 44-SN-0631. SET: MARK 9 ACTIVE. BEARING CHANNEL: GOOD. RANGE FIELD: EMPTY, 6 RETURNS. CAUSE: TARGET EXTENT ABOVE PARAMETER. CLASS: SENSOR PARAMETER EXCEPTION. ACTION: NONE. PARAMETER: UNCHANGED.
en_US.field_note: No action, parameter unchanged. If the range column comes back empty, the set is not broken, it is telling you the contact is bigger than the form allowed for.
en_US.audio:
-- bearing zero nine one. Zero nine one again. Range field is blank. Six returns, six blanks, and this set has not handed me a bearing without a range in four years.

It is not noise. One arc second of scatter across all six.

The gate is throwing the range out as out of parameter and keeping the bearing. It knows where. It will not say how far.

Bearing has walked four degrees in eleven minutes and I have been swimming the whole time. Two hundred metres of my own travel for four degrees of drift. It is holding on me.

Killing the active set. Depth change, not heading. Rook, the extent limit on a Mark 9 is a number somebody chose, and I want that number before anybody crosses here again.
en_US.external_site_article:
Active sonar sets of the Mark 9 generation apply an upper limit on target extent when computing range. A return exceeding that limit fails the range solution, and the set publishes a bearing with an empty range field rather than declaring a fault.

Recovered sensor tickets from HECTON-8 record series of six or more clean returns held on bearing with no range, filed as a sensor parameter exception with no action taken and the parameter left unchanged. Salvage practice treats an empty range field as size information and calls for shutting down the active set.
en_US.external_site: Active sonar sets of the Mark 9 generation apply an upper limit on target extent when computing range. A return exceeding that limit fails the range solution, and the set publishes a bearing with an empty range field rather than declaring a fault.

image_targets.codex: strip of tape at eye height on a doorframe with a shift code, an hour and one word of method written on it, a badge left untouched on the floor below
image_targets.scanner_thumbnail: close view of adhesive tape lettering on painted steel, edges lifting, legible shift code

en_US.title: Marker Inventory, P-63 Back Wall
en_US.scanner: Marauder recorder, recent. Confidence 95 percent. Adhesive marker photographed and transcribed. Limit: original tape not present in this room.
en_US.in_game_wiki:
The tape on a doorframe in Sector 44 is worth more than the contents of the room behind it.

Colony practice was a last-shift marker: shift code, hour, and the method a crew used to leave, taped or scratched at eye height beside the exit they actually took. D-shift, eleven hundred, lower stair on a hand line. Deep Reach recovery listed the markers as personal effects, which kept them out of the safety record and left them on the walls for forty-three years.

Marauder practice is to transcribe one word for word before disturbing anything else in the room.

Three markers in the same hand sit in bays four hundred metres apart, dated the same hour.

Assessment: a marker giving an hour is a tide window. One giving a method is a route somebody survived.
en_US.terminal: RECOVERY LIST 44-PE-2210. ITEMS: ADHESIVE MARKERS, DOORFRAMES, 3. CLASS: PERSONAL EFFECT, NON-RECOVERABLE. SAFETY RECORD: NOT AN ENTRY. BADGES: HELD, RETURN ACTION QUEUE.
en_US.field_note: They listed the warnings as personal effects so the warnings never touched the safety record. Transcribe the tape before you move anything; a badge is sixty grams you cannot spend.
en_US.audio:
-- P-63, back wall, and I am not taking the badge. Third one this month. Tape is still holding and it says D-shift took the lower stair on a hand line at eleven hundred.

That is the item. That is what I carry out.

A badge is a name and a photograph and sixty grams against the window. The tape is a route somebody walked.

Three point one tonnes to make and I am making it out of other people's warnings.

Keel is calling. Word for word, then, before I move anything in here. D dash shift. Eleven hundred. Lower stair, hand line.
en_US.external_site_article:
Colony crews on HECTON-8 marked their exits with a last-shift marker giving a shift code, an hour, and the method used to leave. Examples survive on doorframes in Sector 44, including the Shallow Annex P-63 area, in tape and in scratched paint.

Deep Reach recovery lists classify these markers as personal effects, non-recoverable, which excludes them from the safety record. Marauder crews working the sector transcribe them before disturbing a room, treating a stated hour as a tide window and a stated method as a route with a known outcome.
en_US.external_site: Colony crews on HECTON-8 marked their exits with a last-shift marker giving a shift code, an hour, and the method used to leave. Examples survive on doorframes in Sector 44, including the Shallow Annex P-63 area, in tape and in scratched paint.
